paras: The Osceola murders and threatened lynching took place in late May 1888, when a widow and her teenage son were beaten to death in their cabin four miles from Osceola, Mississippi County, Arkansas, and four men held for the crime were threatened with lynching. The wire called her Mrs. Stokes Allen and the Osceola Times called her Mrs. Mary Warren. Papers across the country predicted that the accused, a Black tenant named John King and three white men, would be hanged by a mob, but no lynching was reported.

On Saturday night, May 26, John King, a Black tenant on W. P. Hale's farm, known as the Witherspoon place, gave a dance at his house. The widow lived about 100 yards away with a son of about 16 and a daughter of 10. Three young white men, Jack Matthews, Tom Field and George Curtis, came to the dance and, by their own account, went to her house around midnight or 1 a.m., knocked, and left when no one answered.

About 3 a.m. on Sunday the daughter came to the Kings' door saying her mother was dead. Mrs. King found the widow dead on the floor and the boy unconscious beside her, and a bloodied plank about four feet long lay nearby. The boy, named Robert in the Memphis Appeal and Bob Taylor in the Osceola Times, died that evening without speaking. The wire said the woman had been ravished and the girl fatally hurt, but the local paper reported that the girl regained consciousness.

The sheriff arrested King, Matthews, Curtis and Fields. According to the Appeal's correspondent, the girl recognized Matthews and said she had seen him, King and another man in the yard after she let her brother in. The wire, carried to Memphis by officers of the steamer Rosa Lee, reported that 'A lynching is certain' and that the four would probably be hanged the next day, while 'conservative people' held off a mob until a full examination. On June 3 the Appeal reported that a mob was being organized and that two prisoners were in a jail guarded by deputies, with a third man at large.

A coroner's jury sat from Sunday to Wednesday night and examined forty or fifty witnesses. It found that Mrs. Mary Warren and her son had died 'by blows from a club in the hands of a person or persons to us unknown,' and King and Matthews were held for a magistrate's court. Memphis reports of June 6 and 8, based on steamboatmen's accounts, still described the jury as sitting and said King had made conflicting statements.

Black residents reportedly sent the sheriff a letter swearing to burn the jail, courthouse and town if King were hanged by a mob. The Osceola Times attributed anonymous letters of that kind to a Black preacher and wrote that he had since felt 'an urgent call to seek another charge.' No report of a lynching, indictment or trial was found.

The Memphis dispatch of May 29 ran within days in Indianapolis, Fort Worth, Wheeling, Austin and Louisville, under headlines such as 'A Monstrous Crime' and 'A Lynching can Hardly be Prevented.' Shorter versions reached weeklies in New Jersey, Wisconsin, Dakota and Nebraska, and one placed Osceola in Tennessee. The Memphis Appeal, which had its own correspondent, gave the fullest account and called the accused 'bloody murderers' who would get 'their just deserts', while the Hickman Courier called them 'fiends' who 'will be lynched.'
The local Osceola Times was more restrained. It printed the inquest testimony and the verdict naming no killer, made no prediction of a lynching, and treated the Black preacher's threat as a joke.

The victim's name differs: the wire gave 'Mrs. Stokes Allen', the local paper gave Mrs. Mary Warren, widow of Stokes Warren, and later Memphis items said 'Mrs. Stokes'. Accounts also differ on the weapon (a plank in most, an axe in the Hickman Courier), the son's age (12 to 17), and whether the daughter would die. The Osceola Times, quoting the jury's verdict, is the nearest source on the name and on the inquest's result.

bases: A widow and her son were murdered by persons unknown and four accused men in jail were threatened with lynching, which was predicted but not reported carried out (A1, A8, A10).

No one was killed by a mob; papers predicted the lynching of the four prisoners and reported a mob organizing (A1, A10), but through June 16 the local paper still wrote of King's lynching as hypothetical (A17).
The Memphis wire, the Appeal's correspondent and the local Osceola Times independently agree on the murders, the four arrests and the threat of lynching (A1, A2, A7, A8).

accounts.gist: Mrs. Mary Warren and her son Bob Taylor were clubbed to death; the coroner's jury found the killers unknown, and King and Matthews were held for a magistrate.

accounts.gist: A mob was organizing on June 2; by June 7 the inquest was reported still sitting, and Black residents had threatened arson if King were lynched.

framing.detail: The Memphis wire ran under headlines such as 'A Monstrous Crime', 'Fiendish Crime ... A Lynching probable' and 'A Lynching can Hardly be Prevented'.
The Memphis Appeal called the accused 'fiends' and 'bloody murderers', said the citizens wanted them to have 'their just deserts', and also reported that conservative counsels prevailed.
The Hickman Courier called the accused 'fiends' and 'three trifling white men' and said they 'will be lynched'.
The Osceola Times reported the inquest testimony and verdict without predicting a lynching, and mocked the Black preacher who wrote the threatening letters.
